match.reason: The closest point, e-lrasshift, covers what shifts long-run aggregate supply in general, while the new point focuses on productivity (output per hour) as the driver of long-term growth, so it is related but narrower and not the same.

draft.title: Aggregate supply and productivity
card: Aggregate supply is the total output that firms in an economy are willing and able to produce. Over the long term, it grows when the economy has more inputs or better inputs.
Inputs include labour, capital (such as machines and buildings), land and natural resources, and enterprise. More workers or more machines can raise output.
Productivity is the output produced per hour of work. Labour productivity rises with better skills, better technology and better equipment.
Higher productivity lets the same hours of work produce more. This is why it is a main driver of long-term growth in living standards, and why it matters more than simply adding more hours.
draft.remember: Long-term growth comes from more inputs and from better ones. Productivity is output per hour of work.

a.q: Which change would directly raise labour productivity in a bakery?
opts: Staff train to use a faster, more efficient oven
The bakery hires two extra workers on the same ovens
The bakery stays open for two more hours each day
The bakery's customers increase their spending
a.why: Labour productivity is output per hour of work, so a better oven lets each hour produce more. Hiring workers or opening longer adds hours and may raise total output, but it does not raise output per hour.
a.clue: Look for the change that raises output per hour, not total hours.

b.q: Country X's output rises 4% in a year because its workforce works 4% more hours in total. What can be said about its labour productivity?
opts: It did not change, as output per hour stayed the same
It rose by 4%, as total output rose by 4%
It fell, because more workers were needed
It rose, because the economy has more inputs
b.why: Output and hours both rose 4%, so output per hour stayed the same. The growth came from more labour input, not better output per hour. Total output rising does not on its own mean productivity rose.
b.clue: Divide output by hours worked, and see what happens to the result.

a.best: Staff train to use a faster, more efficient oven

b.best: It did not change, as output per hour stayed the same
